blocks.text:
David Mcgee
General Manager
Hicks-Castillo
Dear David,

Thank you for asking us to take on your compensation benchmarking. This letter sets out how we will carry out that work for {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}}, and the terms we will work under. We treat a retained engagement as a partnership. So we like to begin with everything written down plainly, before any of the work starts, and this letter is that beginning.
The Work You Have Asked Us to Do

You want to know, with confidence, where the pay of your senior team sits against the companies you actually compete with for that talent. It is a fair question and a harder one than it sounds, because a good comparison depends entirely on choosing the right peers and reading the numbers honestly. Our task is to gather that market data with care, to test it against what we see in our own placement work, and to bring you a picture you and your board can act on. We work on a retained basis. That means we work for you alone on this study, and we stay with it until the findings are in your hands and you have had the chance to talk them through with us.
The study moves through a few clear stages, and I want you to know the shape of it from the first day.

items: First, we agree the scope with you: the roles in view, the peer group we will measure you against, and the questions your board most wants answered.
Second, we assemble the market data, drawing on both the published compensation surveys and what we learn firsthand placing senior people, and we clean it so that every comparison is a fair one.
Third, we analyze the findings role by role, across base pay, incentive, and total compensation, so that nothing hides inside a single blended number.
Fourth, we bring you a written report, and we sit with you and your board to walk through what it means and where you may want to act.

blocks.text: None of this is guesswork. The value of a benchmark comes entirely from the honesty of the comparison behind it, and most of our effort goes into getting that comparison right before a single figure reaches your board. A smaller set of numbers we can stand behind completely will serve you better than a thick report no one can quite trust, and that is the standard we hold ourselves to.
Who Will Do the Work

I will oversee this engagement myself, and I remain your point of contact whenever you want one. Sandra Fuentes, a Principal in our practice, will lead the study day to day and own the relationship with you from the first conversation to the last. David Weiss, a Research Associate on our bench, will do the market research and the careful data-gathering the whole study rests on. It is a small team by design. You will always know who is doing your work, and you will rarely have to explain yourself twice.
Our Fee, and When We Begin

For a study of this kind we work to a fixed professional fee of {{fact:f:E-2023-001.fee}}. That fee covers the whole of the work, from the scoping conversation through to the final report and our presentation of it to your board. It does not move with the size of the findings or the hours the work takes. You know the cost at the outset. We expect to begin on {{fact:f:E-2023-001.start}}, and the study runs for something on the order of eight months from there, allowing for the survey cycles that the good comparisons depend on.
Fees and Payment

We bill the fixed fee in three parts, tied to the milestones of the study: on your signing of this letter, on the delivery of our draft findings, and on the final report. Invoices are due on receipt. Any reasonable direct cost we arrange at your request, such as a purchased survey your board specifically wants included, we pass through at cost and only with your agreement in advance, so nothing on an invoice is ever a surprise.
The Length of the Engagement, and Ending It

The engagement runs from your signature until the report is delivered and our final invoice is settled. Either of us may end it sooner, in writing. We ask only for a short conversation first, so that nothing ends on a misunderstanding. If you close the study early for a reason unrelated to our work, we bill for the work done to that point and no more.
Holding Confidence

Compensation is the most guarded number a company keeps, and we treat it that way. What you tell us about your own pay, and everything we assemble about the market, stays confidential and is used only for this work. Inside our office, access sits with the people named above and with anyone whose work on the study requires it. We extend the same care to the comparator data. We report the market in aggregate, never in a way that would expose what any one company pays a named person.
Where Our Liability Sits

We give this study our best professional judgment, and we stand behind the care we take. Still, the compensation decisions you make from our findings are finally yours, and we cannot warrant the outcome of choices we do not control. Our liability to you under this engagement, whether framed in contract or in negligence, will not exceed the total fees you pay us for the work.
The Law That Governs Us

This agreement is governed by the law of the state in which our office sits, without regard to its conflict-of-laws rules. Should any dispute arise, we will each make a genuine effort to settle it in conversation before either of us turns anywhere else.

If these terms read as we agreed them, the next step is a simple one. Please sign both copies where shown below, keep one for your file, and send the other back to me. That single signature is all we need to begin. If anything here gives you pause, call me first, and we will settle it before you sign.
With warm regards,
Engagement Kickoff

To: Sandra Fuentes, Heather Meyer
From: David Weiss
Re: Compensation benchmarking for Hicks-Castillo, engagement kickoff

The objective of this engagement is straightforward, and it is worth stating before anything else: we are to give {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}} a defensible, role-by-role picture of where its senior compensation stands against a peer group we can stand behind. Everything we do over the coming months serves that single end, and every choice we make about data and method should be judged against whether it makes that picture more honest or less. The engagement is now under way as of {{fact:f:E-2023-001.start}}, and our client contact throughout is David Mcgee, the General Manager, who has asked for findings his board can act on rather than a survey dump.

Sandra Fuentes leads the engagement and owns the client relationship, while the two of us on the research bench carry the data. Because the quality of a benchmark lives entirely in the peer group and the cleanliness of the underlying figures, the early phase is where a study like this is won or lost, and that is where our attention has to go first, before any figure is pulled.

The client's concern, as David Mcgee framed it at the outset, is competitive: he believes the company may be losing operating leaders on pay and wants to know whether that instinct is borne out by the market before the board sets next year's compensation. That gives the study a clear question to answer, and it tells us where to press hardest, on incentive and total compensation for the operating-leader roles rather than on base pay taken alone.
The Work Ahead

items: Scope and peer group: with Sandra, confirm the roles in view and assemble a defensible list of comparator companies, so that every later number rests on an agreed foundation.

Survey and source assembly: gather the relevant published compensation surveys for the sectors and geographies in scope, and log each source with its date and coverage so the analysis stays auditable.
Firsthand market read: draw on what the firm sees directly in placing senior operators, treated in aggregate, to sense-check the published figures against a live market.
Normalization: reconcile titles, role scope, and pay definitions across sources, because a general manager in one survey is not always a general manager in another.
Analysis and drafting: build the role-by-role comparison across base, incentive, and total compensation, and draft the findings for Sandra's review.

blocks.text: A note on sequence: the peer group has to settle before the data build begins in earnest, because rework at that stage is expensive and every downstream number inherits the comparison set. We should hold off on pulling figures until the scope is signed off, however ready the sources look, since a clean start is what keeps the second half calm.
First Steps

items: Heather Meyer to begin the comparator long list this week and circulate a first draft for Sandra's review by the end of next week.
David Weiss to pull the survey inventory and confirm which sources we already hold and which we must acquire, flagging any that need the client's agreement to purchase.
Sandra Fuentes to set the first client checkpoint with David Mcgee so the scope and peer group are agreed before we commit to the data build.

blocks.text: That is enough to start. I will keep a running log of sources and decisions so that anyone picking up a thread can see how we got there. Questions to me.
Working Session Minutes: Compensation Benchmarking for Hicks-Castillo
A working session held at the client's offices to review progress at the midpoint of the study and to align on the shape of the analysis before we build it out. The following were present:

items: Sandra Fuentes, Principal, Northgate Talent Partners
David Weiss, Research Associate, Northgate Talent Partners
David Mcgee, General Manager, Hicks-Castillo

blocks.text: The headline from the session is that we are on track and the peer group is holding up well, which is the single thing that most determines whether the final numbers will be trusted. We walked David Mcgee through the comparator set we have assembled for {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}} and the reasoning behind each inclusion, and he confirmed that the companies match the ones his team competes with for senior talent in practice, with two additions he asked us to weigh before the set is locked.

David Weiss then summarized the state of the data, which is further along than the halfway mark might suggest. The published surveys for the roles in scope are in hand and logged, the firsthand read from the firm's own placement work is assembled in aggregate, and the normalization of titles and pay definitions across sources is under way, which is the slow, unglamorous part of the work that makes the comparisons honest. We were candid with the client that a few of his roles do not map cleanly onto standard survey titles, and we talked through how we mean to handle those before they quietly distort a total.

We also settled how to treat the survey timing, since two of the sources report on a different fiscal calendar than the client's, and comparing across mismatched periods without noting it would quietly weaken an otherwise sound result. David Weiss will annotate those figures as the analysis is built, so the difference stays visible rather than buried, and the client asked us to carry the same caution into anything that eventually reaches the board.

We spent the back half of the session on what the client most wants to be able to decide once the findings are in. David Mcgee was clear that the board's interest is less in a single market-median figure and more in where the company sits on incentive and on total compensation for its operating leaders, and we agreed to shape the analysis and the eventual report around that emphasis. Nothing in that changes the scope we set out under; it simply sharpens where we spend the analytical effort through the second half of the study.
What We Agreed to Do

rows: Finish the title and pay-definition normalization across all sources and flag every role that needs a judgment call
Weigh David Mcgee's two proposed additions to the peer group and confirm whether they belong before the data build hardens
Confirm the internal role list and current pay ranges for the operating-leader roles so our comparison uses the client's real structure

blocks.text: We set no formal next meeting, but agreed to reconvene once the normalization is complete and the first comparative cuts are ready to look at together. Minutes recorded by Sandra Fuentes.
Status Report: Compensation Benchmarking

Prepared for Hicks-Castillo. Prepared by David Weiss, with Sandra Fuentes as engagement lead. This report covers the reporting period just ended and reflects the state of the engagement at its midpoint.
Where the Engagement Stands

The engagement for {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}} is on schedule and has reached its midpoint. The comparator peer group is agreed with the client, the source data is assembled and logged, and the analysis phase is under way. Nothing at this stage puts the timeline or the quality of the findings at risk.

The midpoint is a meaningful marker on a study like this, because most of what determines whether a benchmark can be trusted is decided in the first half, in the choice of peers and the discipline of the source assembly. That work is now done and agreed with the client, which means the second half is a matter of careful analysis on a foundation that has already been validated rather than a scramble to settle open questions late.

This period also included a working session with the client to review progress and confirm the peer group in person. Sandra Fuentes led that session. The client validated the comparator set and raised two additions, both of which we assessed and folded in. That review matters more than it looks, because the peer group is the one input the whole benchmark cannot be corrected for later, and it now carries the client's explicit sign-off.

Work remains within the agreed fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2023-001.fee}}. The engagement is tracking to budget with no variance to report, and we do not foresee any pass-through costs beyond the ones already discussed and agreed.
Completed This Period
The first half of the engagement produced the foundation the analysis will rest on. In summary:

items: Finalized the comparator peer group with the client, including the two additions raised at the midpoint working session, and locked it as the agreed basis for every downstream comparison.

Completed the assembly and logging of the published compensation surveys covering the roles and markets in scope, each recorded with its source, publication date, and coverage, so that every figure in the final report can be traced back to where it came from.

Assembled the firm's own firsthand read of the senior compensation market, in aggregate and with no individual identifiable, drawn from recent placement work, and used it as an independent check on the published surveys.
Advanced the normalization of titles, role scope, and pay definitions across the sources, which is roughly two-thirds complete and on course to finish early in the coming period.

blocks.text: Taken together, the first half leaves us with a validated peer group, a logged and traceable body of source data, and an independent firsthand check against it. That is the whole reason for front-loading the discipline: the figures the board eventually sees will each carry a clear provenance, and none of them will rest on a comparison the client has not already reviewed and agreed.
The Period Ahead
The second half turns that foundation into findings. The planned work is as follows:

items: Complete the normalization and resolve the small number of client roles that do not map cleanly onto any standard survey title, using a documented judgment rather than a forced match.
Build the role-by-role comparison across base pay, short-term incentive, and total compensation, so that no single blended figure hides a difference the board would want to see.
Produce the first draft analytical cuts for Sandra Fuentes to review, in full, before any figure is shared with the client.
Schedule the next client checkpoint once the first comparative cuts are ready, so the client sees the shape of the findings before the report is drafted.

blocks.text: Risks and Watch Items

One item is worth flagging, and it is a question of method rather than schedule. A few of the client's operating-leader roles carry a scope that does not correspond cleanly to any single survey benchmark, and mapping them to a nearest match would introduce a quiet distortion into the totals. We are handling those roles with an explicit, documented judgment call, and we will show the client the reasoning openly when we present the findings rather than presenting a false precision.

No other risks are open at this time. The survey sources we depend on have published on schedule, the client has been prompt and clear on every question of scope, and the fixed fee leaves no commercial question hanging over the work.
The next report will follow the completion of the first full comparative analysis. Any questions on the above can come to me directly, or to Sandra Fuentes.
Minutes: Findings Review, Hicks-Castillo Benchmarking
A working session to review the draft findings and agree what remains before the final report. Held with:

items: Sandra Fuentes, Principal, Northgate Talent Partners
David Weiss, Research Associate, Northgate Talent Partners
David Mcgee, General Manager, Hicks-Castillo

blocks.text: The main outcome of the session is that the draft findings hold together and the client sees his own company in them, which is the test that matters at this stage. We took David Mcgee through the role-by-role comparison for {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}} across base, incentive, and total compensation, and he recognized both the overall picture and the outliers in it, which tells us the peer group and the normalization did the work they were meant to do.

David Weiss then walked through the two operating-leader roles we had flagged earlier as hard to benchmark, and explained the judgment calls we made and documented instead of forcing a false match onto a survey title. David Mcgee accepted the reasoning and, helpfully, gave us a piece of internal context on one of those roles that lets us tighten the comparison further. We agreed that being transparent about those two roles belongs in the report itself, not buried in a footnote, so that the board understands where the numbers are firm and where they rest on judgment.

Much of the substance turned on the incentive gap. The comparison shows the client's operating leaders at or near market on base pay but trailing the peer group on total compensation, and the difference sits almost entirely in the incentive component. David Mcgee had suspected as much, and seeing it laid out role by role gave him something concrete to take to the board, though we were careful to say that the numbers describe the market and do not, on their own, prescribe what the client should do about them.

We also talked about timing for the close. With the analysis all but settled, David Mcgee asked how soon the board could see a final version, and we were straight with him that the two open refinements come first. A benchmark that shifts after the board has already seen it does more damage to confidence than the few days of waiting would ever be worth, so we agreed to hold the presentation until the report is genuinely final.

We closed on how the client wants the findings framed for the board. David Mcgee asked that the report lead with total compensation for the operating leaders and treat base pay as supporting detail, consistent with what the board most cares about, and we agreed that framing. We also agreed to keep the comparator companies unnamed in the board version, identifying them by sector and size band, which protects the confidences under which the data was gathered.
Actions Before the Final Report

rows: Incorporate the new internal context on the flagged role and refresh the affected comparison
Redraft the findings summary to lead with total compensation and prepare the board-ready version with comparators anonymized
Confirm the board meeting date so we can schedule the final presentation

blocks.text: We are close. Once these items are done, the final report and a board presentation are all that remain. Minutes recorded by Sandra Fuentes.
Final Status Report: Compensation Benchmarking
Prepared for Hicks-Castillo. Prepared by David Weiss, with Sandra Fuentes as engagement lead. This is the final status report for the engagement.
Summary

The engagement for {{fact:f:E-2023-001.client}} is complete in substance. The final report has been delivered, the findings have been presented to the board, and the recommendations are in the client's hands. What remains is administrative: the closing invoice and the handover of the source file.

The purpose of this report is to close the engagement cleanly, to record what was delivered against what was agreed, and to leave the client with a clear account of where the numbers are firm and where they rest on documented judgment. There are no open questions of substance and no surprises in the closing.

The work was delivered within the agreed fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2023-001.fee}}, with no overrun and no pass-through charges. The only commercial item outstanding is the final invoice against that fee.
Delivered This Period
The final period turned the analysis into delivered work product. In summary:

items: Completed the role-by-role compensation comparison across base pay, short-term incentive, and total compensation for every role in scope.
Delivered the final written report, including the explicit and documented treatment of the two operating-leader roles that do not map cleanly onto any standard benchmark.

Presented the findings to the board, leading with total compensation for the operating leaders as the client asked, and identifying the comparator companies by sector and size band rather than by name, consistent with the confidences under which the data was gathered.
Handed over the underlying source inventory, so that for every figure in the report the client can see the source, its date, and its coverage.

blocks.text: The board session went as we had hoped. The directors engaged with the total-compensation comparison directly, asked hard questions about the size of the incentive gap and how firm the underlying numbers were, and left with a shared reading of where the company stands rather than a report to work through later. I prepared the comparison material with the bench, and Sandra Fuentes led the discussion in the room, which is the division of labor that has served this engagement from the start.

The handover deserves a note of its own. Every figure in the report ties back to a logged source, and the client now holds that inventory in full. That means the client can rely on the benchmark, test any number in it, and refresh the whole study a year or two from now without depending on us to reconstruct where a figure came from. That auditability was a design choice from the first week, and it is the part of the delivery I am most confident will hold up over time.
Findings, in Brief

The detail belongs in the report, but the shape is worth restating for the record. The client's base pay for its operating leaders sits within the market range, while total compensation runs below the peer median, and the gap is driven mostly by a lighter incentive component than comparable companies carry rather than by base pay. The two roles we had flagged as hard to benchmark were handled by explicit judgment rather than forced comparison, and the report is candid throughout about where a figure is firm and where it rests on that judgment. Where the survey calendars did not line up with the client's own, the affected figures are annotated so no comparison is read across mismatched periods by accident.
Closing Items

items: Issue the final invoice against the agreed fixed fee.
Confirm the client has everything it needs from the source file, and close the engagement record.

blocks.text: Risks

None open. The report is delivered and accepted, the board presentation is given, and nothing on the engagement is unresolved. Should the board decide it wants follow-on work, whether a refresh of the benchmark or a deeper look at the incentive design, that would be a fresh engagement and a new conversation with Sandra Fuentes, not a continuation of this one.

This has been a straightforward engagement to work and a clean one to close, and the credit for that belongs in large part to a client who gave us honest access and candid answers. My thanks to the client for both. Any questions on this report can come to me or to Sandra Fuentes.
